author: Marcus R. Brown
description:
Makes `Fro Bot` a required status check on `main`.

```diff
-        contexts: [Build, Check, Renovate / Renovate, Setup]
+        contexts: [Build, Check, Fro Bot, Renovate / Renovate, Setup]
```

## Why now

It has been advisory since it landed. Over this session it caught eight substantive defects across consecutive PRs, including several I introduced and would otherwise have shipped:

- a `mode: maintenance` dispatch that would have resolved to `branch-pr`, contradicting the prompt's own instruction not to open PRs
- a code-point vs UTF-16 offset divergence in tab completion that corrupted any command line containing an emoji
- three missing regression tests covering behavior changes documented in a PR body but never asserted
- a missing changeset on a published package whose runtime behavior changed

Each was found by independently reproducing the work rather than reading the diff — running the affected suites, checking out the pre-PR file to confirm a failure was pre-existing, introspecting the resolved ESLint config. That is the level of review worth blocking on.

## Why a skipped run does not deadlock

This is the non-obvious part, and it is the reason the check was left advisory until now.

`Fro Bot` is conditional — it skips fork PRs, `[bot]`-authored PRs, and its own PRs via a job-level `if:` at `fro-bot.yaml:628`. GitHub documents that a job skipped by a job-level condition reports its status as **Success** and does not block a required check.

The case that *does* deadlock is workflow-level skipping — `paths`, `paths-ignore`, or `branches` filters, or `[skip ci]` — where no check run is ever posted and the requirement sits at `Expected` indefinitely.

`fro-bot.yaml`'s `on.pull_request` carries only `types:`, with no path or branch filters, so it always posts a check. Verified before making the change, along with the job `name:` matching the context string exactly. [description truncated to fit budget]
title: chore(ci): require the Fro Bot check on main
